title: Cloud access key found in a public code repository at a small company
summary: A cloud access key is found in a public code repository, the cloud bill jumps overnight, and the team must decide whether customer files were copied and who needs to be told. The exercise tests who can revoke a live key and who approves a customer notice.

setting.company_profile: A 30-person company that runs its product in a cloud account, keeps its code on GitHub and stores customer files in cloud storage.
setting.day_and_time: Tuesday, 8:45 a.m., the morning of a product release
setting.initial_signal: The cloud provider emails the account owner: an access key for the company's cloud account has been found in a public GitHub repository.

roles.name: Incident Commander
roles.responsibilities: Runs the response and decides when the leaked key is revoked on release day.

roles.name: Technical Lead
roles.responsibilities: Revokes and replaces the key and reports what the cloud account's logs show.

roles.name: Communications Lead
roles.responsibilities: Drafts what customer support and affected customers are told.

roles.name: Scribe
roles.responsibilities: Keeps a timed record of findings, decisions and owners.

objectives: Decide who can revoke a production access key during business hours.
Confirm the team can find out what a leaked key was used for.
Name who approves a notice to customers and who tracks the deadline.

injects.title: The cloud provider reports an exposed key
injects.narrative: At 8:45 a.m. the cloud provider emails the account owner: an access key for the company's cloud account has been found in a public GitHub repository created by one of its developers. The key is still active. A product release is planned for 11:00 a.m. and the developer is in a meeting.
questions: Who declares an incident, and who is told first?
Does the 11:00 a.m. release go ahead while this is open, and who decides?
expected_actions: Name an Incident Commander and open a dedicated channel for the response.
Ask the developer to make the repository private without deleting it.

injects.title: The key is used by the live product
injects.narrative: The key belongs to the service that stores customer uploads. Revoking it will interrupt uploads for about an hour while a replacement is rolled out. The head of product asks whether this can wait until the evening, after the release.
questions: Who has the authority to revoke the key now and accept an hour of interrupted uploads?
Who tells customer support what to expect?
expected_actions: Revoke the key in the cloud console and issue a replacement with only the permissions the service needs.
Post a note for customer support with the expected length of the interruption.

injects.title: An unexpected bill
injects.narrative: The billing page shows $4,200 of new charges since yesterday for servers in a region the company does not use. The account's activity log shows the leaked key started them. Finance asks whether the company has to pay.
questions: Who shuts the servers down, and what is recorded first?
Who contacts the cloud provider about the charges?
expected_actions: Record the server IDs and start times, then stop the servers.
Open a support case with the cloud provider reporting the compromised key and the charges.

injects.title: Were customer files read?
injects.narrative: Storage logs show the leaked key read files in the customer uploads folder overnight. Logging was only switched on two weeks ago, so nobody can say what normal looks like. One customer contract requires notice within 72 hours of a suspected breach.
questions: Does the team treat the files as accessed, and who decides?
Who tracks the 72-hour deadline, and who approves the notice?
expected_actions: Record a working assumption that the files were accessed and list the customers affected.
Send the contract clause to outside counsel and name an owner for the deadline.

injects.title: Closing the incident
injects.narrative: The replacement key is in place and the unknown servers are stopped. A customer who saw the repository mentioned online emails to ask what happened. The team wants to close the incident and get back to the release.
questions: Who replies to the customer, and what can be said today?
Who declares the incident closed, and what must be true first?
expected_actions: Send the customer a factual reply approved by the Incident Commander, with a time for the next update.
Search every repository for other keys and book a review of the plan.

wrap_up_questions: Which decisions did the plan answer, and which did the team improvise?
What information or access was missing when the team needed it?
What will change in the plan as a result?
Who owns each change, and by what date?
